themes.name: No Ground Truth to Measure Against
themes.plain: Most of these problems have no answer key. There is no stable number to grade your work against, and the thing being measured often moves while you measure it, so the models start by building a small truth set of their own or admit the number is only an estimate.
themes.evidence: On answer engine optimization all three models build a fixed panel of real buyer questions because answers are stochastic and personalized; on identity resolution Claude recruits a consenting panel as a truth set, on incrementality the models run standing geo holdouts, and on B2B buying-group signal they note a degraded signal and a signal that was never real look identical.

themes.name: Nobody Can Verify Downstream
themes.plain: Once data, a message, or a dollar leaves your own systems, you cannot see inside the partner, ad platform, or trained model that now holds it. You can watch from outside and guess whether the rules were followed, but you cannot prove it.
themes.evidence: On provable downstream consent and deletion, all three models say proof ends at the perimeter: ad platforms are black boxes, and a model that learned from a person cannot unlearn them without retraining, which echoes platforms concealing treatment in incrementality and vendors hiding effects in safe agent execution.

themes.name: Chokepoint Before Trust
themes.plain: When the models cannot trust who is acting or what happens next, they build one door they own and push everything through it. A sent email, a spent dollar, or an exported file cannot be taken back, so the only real control happens before the action leaves.
themes.evidence: On safe agent execution every model puts a proxy or gateway in front of writes with hard spend, rate, and audience caps; on downstream consent they inventory every exit and gate it, and on journey orchestration they build one shared contact log that can say no before a send.

themes.name: Incentives Before Standards
themes.plain: Many of these problems stall because the people holding the answer gain nothing by sharing it, and nobody can force them. The blockers are money and politics, inside the company as much as outside, so the models try to make honesty or cooperation pay rather than write another rule.
themes.evidence: On agentic traffic the models build a fast declared-agent lane because agents profit by looking human; on journey orchestration channel owners are paid for sends they would have to give up; on the semantic context layer all three call conflicting definitions of customer a political settlement, and on ad supply integrity the parties measuring fraud often profit from the traffic.

themes.name: Judgment That Won't Compile
themes.plain: The hardest calls turn on meaning and context: whether a picture plus a headline implies a promise, whether evidence really backs a claim, whether two teams can both be right about what a word means. No rule set captures that, so the models shrink human judgment into a smaller, safer box instead of removing it.
themes.evidence: On generative content governance all three build an approved-claim registry and constrain what the model may say, while naming implied meaning and context as the part software cannot judge; on the semantic context layer they argue legitimate competing definitions must be disclosed rather than collapsed into one.
